title: Inside the Bell at Kerrig
passage:
A bell that has just come out of its mould sits sharp, and at Kerrig that is deliberate. On the lathe in the far bay a bell of two hundred and forty kilos, cast for the parish of Larrowden, turns slowly on its side while Matthias Voregg draws a long curl of bronze off the inner wall and the note it will hold for the next two centuries settles a few cents lower. A bell is not one note but a stack of them. The tuners here work with five: the hum, lowest and longest-lasting; the prime above it; then a minor third, a fifth, and the nominal, an octave over the prime. What a listener hears as the bell's pitch is not quite any of these; it is something the ear assembles out of the upper partials, which is why a bell can be in tune with itself and still quarrel with the bell hanging beside it. Each partial answers to a band of metal at a particular height inside the bell, and thinning that band pulls the partial down. Nothing pulls it back up.

That one-way arrow is why founders cast heavy. A bell leaves the mould thicker and sharper than the drawing asks for, carrying an allowance of metal — twelve kilos on the Larrowden bell, against a finished weight of two hundred and twenty-eight — that exists only to be turned away. The turnings are not lost. They go back into the melt, and a foundry that keeps its bins swept recovers most of what the lathe takes off. Most, not all: bronze cut fine and left to the air gives up a little of its tin at the next pour, and the alloy has to be brought back with new metal. That correction is cheap. Lathe time is not, and it does not scale the way metal does, because a founder bills bronze by the kilo and tuning by the hour. On a thirty-kilo bell the tuning can come to more than half of what the parish pays; on a bell of a tonne, where the same five partials take not much longer to find, the bronze is the larger part of the bill.

How far to chase those five is where the trade divides. Voregg brings all of them inside four cents of the figures the theory gives, and can name the tolerance on any bell that has left his yard since 1994. Vivienne Corvenden, who runs the Vennerby works two valleys away, thinks this is a habit learned from instruments rather than from ringing. She tunes the hum, the prime and the nominal closely and leaves the minor third near where the casting put it, on the argument that the last few cents are bought by thinning one band unevenly against its neighbours, and that a wall shaved in that way loses body and holds its sound for a shorter time, however well it measures afterwards. "You can hear a bell that has been argued with," she says.

There is some evidence for her, and Voregg does not pretend there is not. When the ringers' guild at Ockthorne hung eleven bells behind a screen in 2019 and asked forty-odd ringers which they would keep, Vennerby bells took six of the first seven places, and the most exactly tuned bell in the trial came ninth. "One afternoon, one tower, bells of different weights," Voregg says. "I would not build a workshop on that. I would not throw it away either." He adds, reasonably enough, that nobody has yet cast two bells from one mould, hung them together and tuned them differently; the experiment that would settle the question costs two bells, and no parish has ordered it.

None of this reaches the paper a parish signs. The Larrowden order runs to three pages and fixes the weight, the note, the crown fittings and the delivery date; about the partials it says only that the bell shall be tuned on the lathe in the usual manner. Corvenden and Voregg would both meet that clause. They would meet it four kilos apart at the pour and the better part of a day apart on the lathe, and the difference is in the price long before anyone has heard the bell. Under the lathe at Kerrig the bin of turnings from the Larrowden job stands about a third full.
— Callum Illingsby

questions.prompt: What are we told about the cost of casting and tuning a bell?

options.text: Tuning is billed by the hour and always takes a larger share of the price than the metal.

Time on the lathe rises with a bell's weight, so a bell of a tonne takes far longer to tune.

questions.rationale: Family ELF-TYPE-001 (direct detail retrieval), local order, anchored in paragraph 2. WHY-KEY (D): the passage states that "a founder bills bronze by the kilo and tuning by the hour" and then gives the two ends of the range: "On a thirty-kilo bell the tuning can come to more than half of what the parish pays; on a bell of a tonne, where the same five partials take not much longer to find, the bronze is the larger part of the bill." D paraphrases both ends of that flip without lifting a distinctive run. WHY-DISTRACTORS: A = quantifier_upgrade — keeps the true billing detail ("tuning by the hour") but absolutises the share into "always", which the tonne-bell half of the sentence directly contradicts; tempting to a reader who registers only the thirty-kilo example. B = outside_knowledge — a plausible real-world quoting practice (one all-in price per kilo) that the passage contradicts, since bronze and lathe time are billed on different units; tempting because price-per-kilo is the natural way to imagine buying metal. C = reversed scaling — the passage says the opposite, that lathe time "does not scale the way metal does" and that on a tonne bell "the same five partials take not much longer to find"; tempting because it is the intuitive assumption about a bigger object taking proportionally longer.

questions.rationale: Family ELF-TYPE-002 (inference / implication), one logical inch beyond the text. WHY-KEY (A): the passage establishes that thinning "pulls the partial down" and that "Nothing pulls it back up", that this "one-way arrow is why founders cast heavy", and that the Larrowden bell carries "an allowance of metal — twelve kilos" that "exists only to be turned away"; paragraph 5 then reports that Corvenden and Voregg "would meet it four kilos apart at the pour". The inch of inference is that the tighter tolerance has to be provided for at the casting stage, because the allowance cannot be added once the bronze has set. WHY-DISTRACTORS: B = too_literal — it restates the paragraph-1 mechanism ("thinning that band pulls the partial down") rather than drawing any implication, so it is retrieval dressed as inference; tempting because it is unambiguously true. It is also not an answer to this stem: B holds of every bell whether or not anyone chases the partials, so nothing in it turns on the founder's intention, whereas A names what that intention requires at the pour. C = too_far — a two-step leap to fittings and frame, which the passage never connects to tuning at all; tempting because the Larrowden order does list "the crown fittings". D = quantifier_upgrade plus attribution swap — takes Corvenden's argument that a wall shaved for the last cents "loses body" and hardens it into a law about "any" bell, "always"; the passage offers it as her reasoning, and the one trial reported is described by Voregg as "One afternoon, one tower".

questions.rationale: Family ELF-TYPE-005 (stance / tone / attitude), edge-adjacent, signature trap role_or_attribution_swap. HEDGE BALANCE: options A and C are both measured in form, so "pick the only qualified option" does not decide the item; direction and content do. WHY-KEY (C): the writer reports Corvenden's argument in full, then concedes "There is some evidence for her", then reports the Ockthorne result and Voregg's caveat, and endorses only Voregg's point about the state of the evidence — "He adds, reasonably enough, that nobody has yet cast two bells from one mould, hung them together and tuned them differently". No sentence in the passage says which way of tuning is better; both of the writer's evaluative markers — the concession "There is some evidence for her" and the "reasonably enough" attached to Voregg's caveat — are aimed at what the evidence can bear, not at the craft question. WHY-DISTRACTORS: A = direction lean, hedged in form — the concession it builds on is real, since the writer does say "There is some evidence for her", but he stops there and A does not: it promotes the screen test to "the nearest thing to proof", which is the one thing the writer withholds. He reports the trial together with Voregg's discount of it ("One afternoon, one tower, bells of different weights"), calls that discount reasonable, and adds that "the experiment that would settle the question costs two bells, and no parish has ordered it" — so the trial is presented as thin evidence, not as near-proof. B = polarity error — "can never settle" contradicts the passage's explicit statement that a settling experiment exists and is merely unaffordable. D = role_or_attribution_swap in the other direction — assigns Voregg's caution to the writer and turns it into dismissal of Corvenden, which the concession "There is some evidence for her" plainly blocks.

FRAME BALANCE: all four options are wh-topic frames and the openers split two and two (How / Why / Why / How), so no option is the odd one out by shape and "pick the option that is built differently" does not decide the item; content does. WHY-KEY (D): the passage moves from the mechanism (five partials, each lowered by thinning a band, "Nothing pulls it back up") to the money it implies (the cast-in allowance, the recovered turnings, "a founder bills bronze by the kilo and tuning by the hour") to the open question of tolerance ("How far to chase those five is where the trade divides"). D names all three strands without asserting a verdict the text does not reach. WHY-DISTRACTORS: A = scope_error — promotes one half of the paragraph-2 cost comparison to the whole point ("largely decide the price a parish pays"), and gets it wrong at the top of the range, where "the bronze is the larger part of the bill"; tempting because lathe hours are the passage's most concrete cost. B = surface_word_match — recycles the turnings passage ("recovers most of what the lathe takes off. Most, not all") into a claim about founders misjudging their own recovery, which the text never makes; tempting because the qualification is memorable. C = outside_knowledge — a title-plausible piety about craftsmanship and durability that the passage never argues; tempting because the text does mention a note the bell "will hold for the next two centuries".
